Finally we find that single-target concentration predictions are more accurate than the multiple target predictions for both case studies.
item.dc:creator: Anna Taka, Eleni D. Koronaki, Ioannis G. Kevrekidis, Eike Cramer, Joern Viell, Alexander Mitsos

item.title: GPromptShield: Elevating Resilience in Graph Prompt Tuning against Adversarial Attacks
item.description: The paradigm of ``pre-training and prompt-tuning", with its effectiveness and lightweight characteristics, has rapidly spread from the language field to the graph field. Several pioneering studies have designed specialized prompt functions for diverse downstream graph tasks based on various graph pre-training strategies. These prompts concentrate on the compatibility between the pre-training pretext and downstream graph tasks, aiming to bridge the gap between them. However, designing prompts blindly to adapt to downstream tasks based on this concept neglects crucial security issues. By conducting covert attacks on downstream graph data, we find that even when the downstream task data closely matches that of the pre-training tasks, it is still feasible to generate highly misleading prompts using simple deceptive techniques. In this paper, we shift the primary focus of graph prompts from compatibility to vulnerability issues in adversarial attack scenarios. We design a highly extensible shield defense system for the prompts, which enhances their robustness from two perspectives: Direct Handling and Indirect Amplification. When downstream graph data contains unreliable biases, the former directly combats invalid information by incorporating hybrid multi-defense prompts to the input graph's feature space, while the latter adopts a training strategy to bypass the invalid components and amplifies valid part. We provide a theoretical derivation that proves their feasibility, indicating that unbiased prompts exist under certain conditions on unreliable data. Extensive experiments across various scenarios of adversarial attacks indicate that the prompts within our defense system exhibit enhanced resilience and superiority. This paper explores a new perspective in graph prompt learning, offering a novel option for robust prompt tuning in downstream tasks.
item.dc:creator: Shuhan Song, Ping Li, Ming Dun, Maolei Huang, Huawei Cao, Xiaochun Ye

item.title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
item.description: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.
item.dc:creator: Benhao Huang, Chaitanya Dwivedi, Xuezhe Ma, Alexander Moreno, Hector Liu

item.title: Conditional Optimal Transport and Triangular Maps for Imitation Learning
item.description: We introduce a unified formulation of imitation learning from demonstrations as a conditional sampling problem solved by triangular transport: a policy is the second block of a triangular map that transports a reference distribution to the conditional distribution of the action chunk given the observation history. Unlike in Diffusion Policy, where it is a fixed Gaussian, the reference becomes a design variable; we take it to be the empirical distribution of the demonstrated action chunks and introduce three instances of the formulation: an optimal transport policy (OTP), a flow matching policy (FMP), and a stochastic interpolant policy (SIP). On the Push-T and robomimic Square tasks, the three policies are competitive in task performance with Diffusion Policy and Consistency Policy while using considerably smaller networks and shorter training, and the informative reference accounts for a substantial part of their performance when few network evaluations are used. The three instances offer different trade-offs rather than a single best method: OTP generates an action chunk with a single evaluation of the smallest network (0.23 million parameters on Push-T) and is suitable for settings in which inference time and model size matter, whereas SIP attains the highest scores among the proposed policies at a higher cost.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Al-Jarrah, Yuhang Mei, Karen Leung, Bamdad Hosseini, Amirhossein Taghvaei

item.title: How Should Parallel Langevin Chains Share Noise?
item.description: Parallel Langevin sampling usually draws an array of independent Gaussian vectors, one row per chain. The average row drives the ensemble mean, with variance $1/K$ per coordinate for $K$ chains. Yet the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) specifies only each row's distribution. Subtracting the column means and rescaling, as in classical antithetic sampling, makes that variance zero. Each chain keeps its ordinary ULA path law for any finite run. For quadratic targets we derive the joint covariance of linear estimates computed from the ensemble mean, including coefficient estimates, time averages and predictions. The identity separates contributions from initial states and Gaussian draws. The coupling changes the second through one scalar, which is zero whenever the draws sum to zero across chains. For nonquadratic targets we bound the remaining variance. Centering has a price: for a quadratic form in the mean-subtracted Gaussian state, the ensemble average has variance $1/(K-1)$ relative to one chain, compared with $1/K$ under independent draws. On three tempered logistic posteriors, eight centered chains reduced the variance of the posterior-mean estimate, summed over coordinates, by two to three orders of magnitude compared with eight independent chains. They also beat 128 independent chains on variance and on variance times sampling time. Under Metropolis correction the reduction shrank to about three- to eightfold: rejected draws no longer balance accepted ones. The measured variance ratios were consistent with a leading-order prediction from rejection frequency and noise energy.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Farell

item.title: RIFT: Reward Improvement Field Transfer for Cross-Domain Offline RL
item.description: Learning from limited target data is a central challenge in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning. Abundant source data can help, but dynamics differences can make direct transition reuse unreliable. We propose Reward Improvement Field Transfer (RIFT), which instead learns how low- and high-reward source transitions differ. RIFT encodes source and target transitions in a shared latent space, pairs low- and high-reward source transitions using optimal transport, and fits an affine field to their displacements. It applies this field to low-reward target anchors and decodes the results to augment the target dataset. The approach builds on the hypothesis that related domains can share useful low-to-high reward structure despite different dynamics. We bound synthesis error under shared class geometry, identify conditions favoring target anchoring over source-high transplant, and derive a conditional connection to downstream return. Experiments on dense-reward locomotion tasks under gravity, morphology, and friction shifts show improved aggregate performance over existing baselines.
item.dc:creator: Jinhee Won, Mardavij Roozbehani, Munther Dahleh

item.title: With the Right Representation, Classical Machine Learning Rivals Deep Models for Olfactory Mixture Similarity
item.description: Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. However, prior comparisons between deep and classical approaches also varied how the relationship between the two mixtures was represented, since the classical baselines primarily relied on weak representations that described each mixture independently and provided little direct signal about how the mixtures differed. In this work, we revisit classical learning using explicit symmetric comparison features on unordered pairs of mixtures, evaluating these representations with XGBoost and kernel ridge regression (KRR). We find that XGBoost with explicit comparison features achieves performance competitive with specialized deep mixture models on the main benchmark. Ablation studies show that coordinate-wise absolute differences alone provide strong predictive performance, while combining them with sums and products yields further improvements. KRR also benefits substantially from explicit comparison features, with further gains from appropriate kernel choice and preprocessing. Overall, these results suggest that explicitly encoding how two mixtures differ is an important ingredient for classical machine learning in low-data olfactory mixture prediction.
item.dc:creator: Ze Dong, Yi Wang, Ambuj Tewari

item.title: Multi-Objective Causal Bandits: Minimal Intervention Space and Policy-Level Learning
item.description: Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. We study multi-objective causal bandits with multiple reward nodes, where actions correspond to interventions on subsets of variables in a causal graph and performance is evaluated through Pareto optimality. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Qasim Elahi, Mahsa Ghasemi, Murat Kocaoglu

item.title: SLiDE: Structured Linear Dynamics for Forecasting with Exogenous Inputs
item.description: Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize under shifts in these inputs. We propose SLiDE, a Koopman-inspired architecture for forecasting with exogenous inputs that imposes structure on latent temporal dynamics. SLiDE approximates nonlinear system evolution using a learned linear operator in a latent space, combining (i) a history encoder that reconstructs the current latent state from past targets and inputs with (ii) a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables. By enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction, SLiDE aligns how past information is encoded with how future states evolve, reducing parameterization and preventing reliance on spurious correlations in the input history. Empirically, SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world benchmarks, including electricity price forecasting and retail demand, while maintaining a computational footprint comparable to lightweight MLP architectures. SLiDE is especially effective at generalizing to shifted exogenous inputs, reducing MSE by 20% on electricity price samples with out-of-range exogenous values and MAE by 30% in a synthetic transfer setting where the same dynamical system is driven by an unseen exogenous process. Ablations confirm the importance of both the structured history encoder and the linear latent rollout, suggesting that structured latent linear dynamics provide a useful inductive bias for forecasting with exogenous inputs.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian P\"utz, Theodore Glavas, Benjamin Sch\"afer, Boris N. Oreshkin, Mark Coates

item.title: LogT: Logically Think with Images for Visual Search
item.description: Thinking with images empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to use an external Zoom-in tool for fine-grained visual search. Recent works employ supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) with tool-specific designs to enable such capabilities. However, achieving logical reasoning alongside accurate and efficient tool use remains a significant challenge. To address this, we shift the focus away from increasing RL complexity and instead identify SFT data quality as a key bottleneck. We then propose LogT (short for Logically Think with Images), a fully automated SFT data engine that explicitly enforces logic-chain-guided reasoning. LogT generates an SFT dataset featuring challenging, visually grounded questions and structured tool-use traces with human-like logic. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two base models, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3.5-8B, on the dataset and evaluating them across seven benchmark test sets. We show that LogT-SFT based on Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the state-of-the-art trained with both SFT and RL, despite using 3.1$\times$ less data and $>120\times$ fewer GPU hours. Furthermore, applying a simple RL recipe without tool-specific design on LogT-SFT yields a model that surpasses prior methods with complex RL setups by a substantial 9.59-point margin. In addition to strong performance gains, our model exhibits higher tool-use accuracy and efficiency, as well as more structured and logically consistent reasoning traces, directly validating the effectiveness of our approach.
item.dc:creator: Yanjun Fu, Quanzeng You, Jiadong Guo, Yujie Lu, Sai Charitha Akula, Haiping Wu, Miao Liu, Sanghamitra Dutta, Lu Yuan

item.title: Revealing the Biases of Large Language Models By Inferring Prior Distributions
item.description: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been known to exhibit a wide range of social biases including name-nationality associations, occupation-gender associations and racial stereotypes. Existing approaches to evaluating these biases typically involve measuring surface-level behavior where a model is fed a dataset of prompts and its outputs are scored relative to ground-truth answers. Inspired by prior elicitation in cognitive science, we propose a different perspective that reconstructs latent bias as a prior underlying the model's behavior. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem where, given prompt-response observations on a bias benchmark dataset, we infer a low-dimensional latent distribution that summarizes the model's stereotyping tendencies. This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Ryo Cheng, Thomas L. Griffiths, Jake C. Snell

item.title: SLICES: A Benchmark and Evaluation Framework for Self-Supervised Learning on Sparse ICU Time Series
item.description: Self-supervised learning (SSL) results for intensive care unit (ICU) time series are hard to compare when data processing, encoders, and adaptation vary together. We present SLICES, a benchmark and evaluation framework for comparing and extending SSL methods under a shared clinical setup. It fixes 24-hour value and observation-mask inputs, a Transformer encoder, patient-level splits, four endpoints, two adaptation protocols, and five matched seeds across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and their pooled union. Masked autoencoding (MAE), joint-embedding prediction (JEPA), and contrastive learning provide reference implementations. Among these objectives, MAE leads mean AUPRC in all nine frozen classification comparisons, also under converged probes, and in seven of nine fine-tuning comparisons. Fine-tuned MAE leads hospital mortality at full labels and scores higher than a supervised Transformer of the same architecture at every label fraction, and SSL fine-tuning gives the lowest length-of-stay error. Supervised baselines remain strong elsewhere: GRU-D leads 24-hour mortality and XGBoost leads acute kidney injury in all three regimes. Rankings depend on the adaptation protocol, the comparator set, and whether the probe loss matches the metric. A two-seed MIMIC-IV rerun with the maintained code stays within two across-seed SDs of the reference in all 48 downstream runs. The code repository supports new objectives, shared downstream evaluation, and regeneration of the reference results, so new SSL methods can be compared with these references under the same conditions. Generalization to unseen hospitals is not tested here and is the natural next extension.
item.dc:creator: Hannes Ill, Dimitrios Proios, Leo Anthony Celi, Peter J. Sch\"uffler

item.title: Recovered or Memorized? Investigating Dynamical Consistency and Faithfulness in World Model Latents
item.description: World models develop internal simulators that can learn the structure and dynamics of an environment. It has been demonstrated that their internal representations are both meaningful and causal, but are these representations faithful to the governing dynamics of the environment they are learning? We introduce Anchored Recovery Certification (ARC), a procedure that utilizes a discrete Fr\'echet distance calculation with ground truth to evaluate dynamical consistency on candidate world models up to an affine gauge. We use the procedure on TD-MPC2 (decoder-free world model) that has learned the pendulum swing on an observation lift under varying hyperparameters at k = 5, 10, 25 steps. The model is then steered within a PCA-derived intervention subspace and compared against a ground-truth simulator using relative error to investigate dynamical faithfulness. ARC sufficiency held for TD-MPC2 most consistently at k = 10, with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, while the relative error between the simulator and the causal latent remained substantial. Further research could be conducted with decoder world models such as DreamerV3 (reconstruction loss) to investigate whether the results differ.
item.dc:creator: Jerome Francisco, Kyle Deng, George Flint, Kevin Zhu

item.title: Check Token: Real-Time Self-Verification and Precise Truncation in LLM Reasoning
item.description: ECC memory embeds 8 parity bits for every 64 data bits and automatically detects and corrects errors on each read. The parity bits carry no data and only safeguard integrity, at ~12.5% overhead. Yet the reasoning chains of large language models lack such built-in self-verification: once an error occurs it propagates along the chain, and existing methods can only verify externally after generation completes. We propose the check token, establishing built-in self-verification for language model generation streams for the first time: a functional marker is added to the vocabulary, and the model triggers self-checking (analysis, localization, truncation, rewriting) by outputting it at any position. The check token carries no reasoning content (discarded after triggering) and only safeguards reasoning correctness, directly corresponding to the role of ECC parity bits, also at only ~13% overhead. Speculative forking further eliminates false-positive latency, and segmented reward makes trigger timing end-to-end learnable. Experiments (Qwen3-32B / Qwen3-Next) show that the check token achieves +10.8 pp improvement on HMMT25 at 1.13x overhead, with token efficiency 88x that of Best-of-8, and the precise truncation advantage monotonically increases with chain length.
item.dc:creator: Fei Ding, Yongkang Zhang, Yuhao Liao, Zijian Zeng, Huiming Yang

item.title: A Crowd-Audited Atlas of Implicit Bias in LLM-Powered Agents
item.description: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.
item.dc:creator: Jason Alexander, Yuxuan Li, Michael Licamele, Wesley Hanwen Deng, Sauvik Das

item.title: TrainExplorer: Autonomous LLM Post-Training via Plan-and-Decouple Exploration
item.description: LLM-based agents can automate model post-training, accelerating progress toward recursive self-improvement. Despite their promise, existing approaches remain under-explored and face two main challenges: (1) strategy lock-in that limits exploration beyond the initial strategy; and (2) coupled execution that obscures the effects of individual modifications. To address these challanges, we propose TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous post-training, that incorporates strategy planning and execution decoupling, to achieve broaden strategy exploration. First, strategy planning draws on scientific literature to construct a candidate search space of training strategies. Then, decoupled execution enables single-component interventions and attribution to guide strategy exploration. Extensive experiments on PostTrainBench demonstrate that TrainExplorer achieves a weighted aggregate score of 39.02, outperforming Claude Code using the same LLM by 7.32 and surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex, which scores 36.23. Code will be available.
item.dc:creator: Xuannan Liu, Tian Lan, Zekun Li, Xing Cui, Zhengfeng Yu, Feihu Jiang, Qianghuai Jia, Longyue Wang, Zhao Xu, Weihua Luo, Peipei Li, Ran He

item.title: Empowering Masked Diffusion Models to Self-Correct with Leave-One-Out Transformers
item.description: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for language modeling, enabling parallel token generation with competitive performance. Yet standard MDMs suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) inability to revise tokens, and (2) sparse training signal. We revisit hollow transformers, which address both limitations by predicting each token from its surrounding context, independently of the input at that position. We introduce the Leave-One-Out Transformer (LOOT), a more efficient and expressive architecture that advances hollow transformers through two complementary advances. First, we redesign the merging mechanism to enable frequent interaction between left and right contexts, substantially improving predictive performance over prior hollow transformers. Second, we derive a lower-variance estimator of the MDM NELBO that supervises all tokens and improves validation perplexity. Together, these advances yield a competitive standalone diffusion language model capable of effective self-correction during inference. On LM1B, LOOT matches the strongest dense-supervision MDM baseline in validation perplexity. On OpenWebText, LOOT achieves higher MAUVE and better generation quality-diversity tradeoffs than prior remasking methods, using $8\times$ fewer forward evaluations and $3.5\times$ fewer inference FLOPs.
item.dc:creator: Sofian Zalouk, Vincent Counathe, Paul J\"unger, Daniel Cao, Daniel Zlotnick, Kilian Q. Weinberger, Christopher De Sa

item.title: Simplify, Agree, Distill: Label-Free Self-Distillation with Stepping Stones
item.description: Can a language model teach itself to reason without labels? On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the model as its own teacher, but strengthens that teacher with a ground-truth solution. The natural label-free substitute, voting over the model's attempts, fails precisely on hard problems: attempts disagree, and their most common answer is often wrong. We propose STONE, a label-free alternative that moves agreement to easier related problems. The model writes these stepping stones, keeps those it solves consistently, and shows the teacher their worked solutions, with final answers removed; the student sees only the original problem. No step reads a label, and inference needs no extra context or model calls. Across five math benchmarks, the proposed method achieves the highest average accuracy for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode. Without thinking mode, it gains 13.2 and 22.7 points, 2.5 and 2.7 times the gains of OPSD with ground-truth solutions.
item.dc:creator: Dingyang Chen, Jinfeng Xiao, Zhenyu Zhang, William Hu, Ziyu Wang, Yang Liu, Shirley Zhang, Yuan Ling, Xinyang Shen, Qi Zhang, Peijie Qiu

item.title: Quantize, Qualify, Rerank: A Recipe for Compressing LLMs Without Losing Quality
item.description: Compressing large language models lowers serving cost, but a single automatic metric may miss quality loss. For the WMT26 Model Compression constrained track, we compress google/gemma-3-12b-it (24.4 GB in bf16) for three translation directions on one H100. Paired bootstrap analysis exposes metric disagreement on 4-bit quantization; guided by WMT24 human meta-evaluation, we use MetricX24-XXL as primary and CometKiwi-XXL as a cross-check. Removing the unused vision stack and non-task vocabulary and using int8 weights or fp8 activations causes no resolved loss, whereas int4 leaves a small residual. QLoRA healing overfits its calibration domain. A Cometoid best-of-4 reranker at $T=0.3$ improves both the 8-bit and 4-bit systems under WMT25 test set. On post-submission WMT26, both remain competitive with bf16 under reference-free metrics; the small difference between the reranked variants is treated as noise.
item.dc:creator: Thamme Gowda

item.title: Embedding Cosine Measures Text Length Before It Measures Homogenization
item.description: Mean pairwise cosine similarity between transformer embeddings is a standard measure of whether online discourse is converging under generative AI. When the embeddings are mean-pooled outputs of an encoder never trained for sentence similarity, this measure mostly tracks text length. In 6.06 million Reddit comments, an uncentered DeBERTa-v3 measure had suggested that only conservative discourse broke toward homogeneity after late 2022. Truncating the same comments from 10 to 150 words raises their mean cosine by eight times the reported break. A placebo that swaps every comment for a random one of equal length reproduces 81% of the asymmetry, and a fixed-content simulation reproduces 78%. The leading principal direction carries 99.9% of raw DeBERTa homogeneity, and once length is handled the asymmetry disappears under every encoder. On 575,000 Stack Exchange answers the measure reports a post-ChatGPT homogenization of technical sites that the placebo fully reproduces, although answers grew longer. A census of 31 studies locates the risk where anisotropic encoders meet time-series or length-unequal designs. A reverse control on a well-known experiment shows that centering with renormalization can reverse a genuine effect. I propose a low-cost diagnostic protocol. Corrected measures show that the two political camps converged between 2019 and 2022 and stopped converging before ChatGPT. Cross-camp replies engage their targets more closely than same-camp replies.
item.dc:creator: Fengming Liu

item.title: A Scalable Multi Task Learning Framework for Modeling Demographic Disagreements in Annotation Tasks
item.description: Annotators from different demographic backgrounds often disagree in systematic ways due to varying lived experiences, cultural contexts, and their relationship to the content. When such disagreement occurs, one group's perspective may sometimes warrant prioritization because they hold an epistemically advantaged standpoint or bear greater stake in the outcome. For example, when assessing toxicity of posts on social media, it may be important to prioritize a targeted group's viewpoint. We propose a Stakeholder-Aware Joint Multi-Task Learning (SAJ-MTL) framework to jointly model demographic disagreement both across- and within- annotator groups. The model uses conditional gradient routing to handle sparsity induced by group-conditional labeling, and parameterization supports customized weighting of groups in different task settings. SAJ-MTL improves group-level performance in toxicity detection through better context-aware understanding of demographic-sensitive content. Only annotator group-membership information is required, which is more practical than existing methods requiring more privacy-invasive individual-level annotator details. Our scalable architecture is also computationally efficient to support large-scale deployment.
item.dc:creator: Soumyajit Gupta, Maria De-Arteaga, Matthew Lease

item.title: Latent Bridge: Asking for Help Without Words
item.description: Text-based model collaboration requires a large model to generate intermediate responses before a smaller model can use its guidance, adding large-model decoding cost to inference. We introduce POND (Prefill-Only, No-Decode), a method that uses a frozen large sender for prefill and a small receiver for all autoregressive decoding. A trainable bridge maps the sender's hidden states to additional attention keys and values, allowing the receiver to use these representations throughout generation. POND also supports periodic review, in which the sender processes the receiver's partial response and updates its guidance through additional prefill passes while preserving the receiver's existing KV cache. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, POND improves receiver performance with senders from different model families. In particular, GLM-5.3 provides gains comparable to those of Qwen3.8-Max when paired with a Qwen receiver, supporting the effectiveness of representation transfer between independently trained model families. POND further demonstrates its ability to generalize across domains. When trained on math and coding tasks, it transfers directly to general knowledge tasks without additional domain-specific training. These results demonstrate that large frontier model prefill representations can improve small-model generation without requiring large-model autoregressive decoding.
item.dc:creator: Qichao Wang, Tingyu Qu, Pengcheng Wu, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Zhiqi Shen, Peilin Zhao, Steven Hoi

item.title: Can LLMs Give Good Product Advice? A Framework for Diagnosing Failures
item.description: Evaluating product advice from a language model requires assessing whether the recommendation meets the user's needs and identifying where the model falls short when it does not. However, matching a product mentioned in an online reply cannot answer either question on its own: several products may be suitable, and the recorded answer may itself be poor advice. When shown a community-listed alternative alongside their own sampled car recommendation, six models prefer the alternative in 1.9 to 6.5 percent of eligible disagreements, consistently across both source-blind presentation orders. We propose a diagnostic framework that separates the user's stated needs, the model's added assumptions, candidate generation, filtering, and final choice, with 19 possible failure modes and the evidence needed to assess them. We apply this framework to product-advice data and to a separate product-selection task with externally assigned relevance labels. The experiments distinguish naming a community-listed product from selecting it and show how answer extraction and candidate-list construction affect the outcome.
item.dc:creator: Assaf Hallak, Yftah Ziser, Gal Chechik

item.title: Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
item.description: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.
item.dc:creator: Roman Makarov, Zhe Xu, Jian Kang

item.title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?
item.description: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.
item.dc:creator: Fangzhi Li, Quan Shi, Wenting Yang, Yueqiao Chen, Jiayu Chang, Shuting Zhao, Zhaowei Xu, Yizhao Chen, Guanchu Wu, Han Xu

item.title: Offline-First Quantized AI: Design and Evaluation of an On-Device Maternal-Health Assistant for Low-Connectivity Environments
item.description: Offline language models could extend access to maternal-health information where internet connectivity is unreliable, but deployment requires both clinically appropriate responses and feasible local execution. This study presents an offline Android assistant integrating ready-made quantized language models, a clinically validated local knowledge package, conversational context, and model-initiated local retrieval. Gemma 4 E2B and Qwen3.5 0.8B were compared across 45 conversations and 312 turns per configuration, including a dedicated offline agentic benchmark. Gemma achieved higher response-quality, context-retention, and safety scores; Qwen offered faster generation and lower memory use. Clinician assessment of 150 Gemma responses across nine clinical domains yielded a mean quality score of 3.80/4, with 147 responses meeting the acceptance criterion. A paired RAG-on/off experiment evaluated 74 questions: retrieval improved 11 responses, left 56 neutral, produced four adverse response changes, and left three pairs unassessable. RAG-on had descriptively higher mean usefulness, safety, correctness, and actionability in the conditional 70-pair subset excluding the four flagged pairs from both conditions. Physical-device testing demonstrated offline responses on a 6 GB Android handset, with a 14.3 s median latency, alongside successful reconnection synchronization in the integrated application. Together, the findings document clinical response quality and practical performance of the integrated offline maternal-health assistant.
item.dc:creator: Okenla AbdulQahhar Abimbola, Maurice Abraham John, Adepoju Jeremiah Moyondafoluwa, Omolaiye Samuel, Oko-Oba Sandra Chioma, Owoo Oluwamayowa Emmanuel, Thanni Adewuyi, Lily Aimas-Love, Benson Eniola, Abdulquddus Ajibade, Sylvia Essessien, Anyanwu Princess Emmanuella, Adereni Abiodun

item.title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
item.description: Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Foley, Jonathan Hartadi, Shivesh Prakash, Hino Wirachapong Suwanphibun, Swapnil Vatsal

item.title: Leakage-aware calibrated decision-level fusion for mental-health text classification
item.description: Decision-level fusion benefits from complementary errors, calibrated probabilities, and leakage-aware evaluation. We evaluated a heterogeneous transformer fusion framework on 262,276 proxy-labeled Reddit records covering anxiety, depression, schizophrenia, and suicidal ideation. In a stratified random split, MinHash-LSH identified 29.1% of test records as lexical near-duplicates of training data. Augmentation-lineage auditing found 50.2% lineage overlap with training, including 30.0% of records retained after lexical filtering. We therefore used lineage-disjoint partitions. Twelve encoders, comprising three seeds each of Bio-ClinicalBERT, MentalBERT, MentalRoBERTa, and RoBERTa-base, underwent cross-fitted validation for calibration and ensemble selection. A class-specific Complementarity Index (CI), defined as the Jaccard distance between members' correctly classified validation sets, was assessed against independent fusion gain. CI correlated with gain for depression (r=0.50) and suicidal ideation (r=0.68), but not anxiety; results for schizophrenia were mixed. The selected MentalBERT, MentalRoBERTa, and RoBERTa-base triad achieved macro-F1 0.844 [0.823, 0.863], MCC 0.779, and ECE 0.0033 after post-fusion recalibration, improving macro-F1 by 0.021 [0.007, 0.037] over the validation-selected best single encoder. Integrated-Gradients attribution diversity was 2.3 times greater in fusion-rescued cases. Removing divergence-driving words destroyed 58% of rescues, versus 12% under random removal. These findings show that lineage auditing detects dependencies missed by lexical filtering, while class-specific complementarity and post-fusion calibration reveal ensemble behavior obscured by aggregate accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Wadii Boulila, Giuseppe Varone, Bilel Benjdira, Maha Driss

item.title: Omni-Workspace: Benchmarking Omni-Modal AI Assistants on Multimodal Workspace Tasks
item.description: Omni-modal agents are expected to move beyond multimodal understanding toward completing complex tasks in realistic multimodal environments. In these settings, information is distributed across heterogeneous files and modalities, with cross-file and cross-modal dependencies requiring agents to continually coordinate perception, reasoning, and tool use as newly gathered evidence informs subsequent actions. However, existing omni-modal benchmarks primarily focus on multimodal perception and understanding, leaving complex task completion through sustained interaction with multimodal workspaces underexplored. We introduce Omni-Workspace, a benchmark comprising 380 deep-research-style tasks across four multimodal workspace types and two difficulty levels. These tasks require agents to inspect and process workspace files, retrieve external information when needed, integrate evidence across files and modalities, and produce artifacts satisfying explicit requirements. Evaluating 18 representative models reveals limitations in long-horizon multimodal workspace execution, with the best model scoring only 65.93 on average. Further analysis identifies multimodal context inflation and task-state drift as recurring challenges. Motivated by these findings, we further propose OmniFocus, a lightweight approach combining multimodal working-memory management with explicit task-state tracking to improve performance and efficiency. Omni-Workspace advances the evaluation and development of omni-modal agents toward autonomous completion of complex tasks in multimodal workspaces.
item.dc:creator: Yuhao Wang, Yucheng Zhao, Yiran Zhong, Feida Zhu, Hongcheng Liu, Qichao Wang, Ming Ma, Yu Wang

item.title: A Bag of Concepts? Testing Role-Filler Binding in the Verbalizable Workspace
item.description: Runtime alignment monitors built on a verbalizable workspace have been proposed as a way to surface a model's silent cognition before it produces output. Their value rests on the workspace carrying enough structure to distinguish safety-relevant propositions, most of which are relational: "the model plans to deceive the user" and "the user plans to deceive the model" share a concept set and differ only in role assignment. We ask whether the workspace carries the role-filler bindings (which entity fills which role) such a monitor would need, on three frontier language models (Qwen3.6-27B, Gemma-3-12B, Gemma-3-27B-IT), under two lens families (J-lens and R-lens), and with two methods for fitting the role direction (difference-of-means and LRE-gradient). We find a clean dissociation: the workspace carries directions that steer what the model outputs about roles but not the representations the model uses to compute them. Linear probes recover role at near-ceiling from the residual stream but score below a rank-matched random control when reading the workspace, and steering the model along the fitted role direction changes which entity it binds to no more than strength-matched control edits do. Ablating the workspace (zeroing the residual stream's projection onto its ten most active lens directions) damages binding on one of the three models (Gemma-3-27B-IT, holding across three lens variants) and shows no binding-specific damage on the other two, with a rank-matched random subspace as the control; this confirms our design detects binding when present, though scale and instruction tuning are confounded there. A workspace-lens monitor built on these directions would therefore miss a role assignment the model itself represents.
item.dc:creator: Reya Dawlah, Elizabeth McMillin, Michael Shihong Zhang, Badrish Ananth, Rishi Adi Ruia, Ane Zu\~niga, Thomas Jiralerspong

item.title: A Systematic Study of Cross-Token Transfer for Data-Efficient Non-Verbal Text-to-Speech
item.description: Non-verbal vocalizations (NVs), such as laughter and breath, carry affective cues that words alone do not convey. Yet NV data remains scarce because speech annotation pipelines often omit or normalize these events. Existing work has improved NV text-to-speech through model design and data curation, but whether one NV token can help a model learn another has received little systematic study. We investigate this cross-token transferability in a controlled CosyVoice 2 setup. We first trace a laughter-only scaling curve, then hold laughter at 200 or 1,600 examples while adding breath, sigh, cough, lip-smack, or neutral speech. With only 200 laughter examples, adding 3,200 cough examples raises end-to-end laughter F1 from 0.170 to 0.529, surpassing the 0.495 obtained from 1,600 laughter examples alone. At the 1,600-example anchor, cough reaches 0.695, nearly matching 6,400 laughter examples (0.697). Waveform-level Whisper-D scoring and a semantic-token transcriber show consistent trends. Cross-token transfer therefore offers a complementary route to low-resource NV generation.
item.dc:creator: Jing Pan, Haibin Wu, Minxue Niu, Florian Metze, Yuzong Liu

item.title: Low-Latency LLM-Based Streaming Multi-Talker ASR with Verifiable Rewards
item.description: LLM-based architectures offer strong generalization and instruction-following capabilities for streaming automatic speech recognition (ASR), but multi-talker use introduces coupled transcription, attribution, and latency challenges. Our wearable setting requires real-time transcription of a conversation between a near-field device wearer and a far-field partner. Because partial hypotheses are rendered on persistent sides of a dialogue UI, speaker roles cannot be permuted and each speaker tag must precede its turn. These sparse tags are weakly optimized by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while committing to a leading tag can delay the text that follows. We therefore post-train a streaming LLM-based ASR model with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), combining a fixed-role Speaker-Attributed WER (SA-WER) grader with a turn-level onset-delay reward. On an eight-direction multi-talker cohort, SA-WER RL reduces SA-WER from $20.51\%$ for SFT to $13.14\%$. Adding the delay objective reduces onset $p50$ by $65\%$ (from $0.918\,\text{s}$ to $0.320\,\text{s}$) and $p90$ by $44\%$ (from $1.389\,\text{s}$ to $0.780\,\text{s}$) relative to SA-WER-only RL, while achieving $12.70\%$ SA-WER. These results demonstrate that fixed-role recognition quality and streaming responsiveness can be improved jointly.
item.dc:creator: Jing Pan, Ruizhi Li, Ju Lin, Jing Zheng, Florian Metze

item.title: What Transfers Across Cuneiform? Script-Level Substrate and Language-Specific Regularities via Segmentation and Representation
item.description: Cuneiform recorded typologically unrelated languages for more than three millennia, raising a natural question: which of its statistical regularities are properties of the shared writing system, and which belong to individual languages? We answer this with two probe pairs targeting the same script-versus-language decomposition. The first compares two unsupervised, dictionary-free segmentation methods: transitional probability (TP), grounded in infant statistical-learning research, and Morfessor. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic evaluation of dictionary-free segmentation on cuneiform; the only prior published baseline relies on a hand-built dictionary (Max-Match, F1 = 0.74). Both our methods reach F1 > 0.97 within language (Morfessor reaches F1 > 0.99 on Akkadian and Sumerian), exceeding MaxMatch by more than 23 F1 points, but diverge sharply in cross-language transfer: TP holds F1 > 0.95 across all six language pairs, while Morfessor collapses to F1 = 0.27 from the 13K-token Elamite source. A learning curve and a Hittite stress test (34.7% foreign-script logograms, where TP drops 35 points and Morfessor only 8) further isolate the two underlying mechanisms. The second probe pair extends the same decomposition to representations: concatenating Unicode and Latin features improves classification in 11 of 12 morphosyntactic tasks (p < 0.01). We release CUNEI-TOOLS and a three-language benchmark.
item.dc:creator: Chuanjun Zhou, Adam G Anderson

item.title: Beyond Binary Audits: Does Guideline Grounding Mitigate Decision-Space Framing in LLM Opioid Prescribing?
item.description: Audits of LLMs for bias in opioid prescribing have largely relied on binary treatment decisions, a signal that current models have saturated. We introduce Q-Pain++, a full-factorial stress test that holds clinical content fixed while independently varying clinical risk factors and the granularity of the available dosage options. Adding an intermediate dosage option to otherwise unchanged vignettes substantially lowers agreement with expert-annotated dosages for most models, while demographic differences in dosage decisions remain small in all but one configuration once clinical risk factors are added. Grounding models in perioperative guidelines through retrieval reduces this framing effect on average but does not eliminate it, and one model's treatment decisions change when the retrieved passages are reordered. These results suggest that audits should vary the answer format, not only patient identity. We will release our codebase as well as Guideline-RAG-associated resources on GitHub (https://github.com/su-boussard-lab/llm-guideline-grounding-opioids).
item.dc:creator: Soumyadeep Roy, Keyi Yu, Tina Hernandez-Boussard

item.title: Assisting Patients with Reliable Information Gathering: A Guide to Building Efficient QA Systems for Medical Use
item.description: The application of question-answering (QA) systems in the medical domain has rapidly advanced, significantly improving patients' access to reliable health-related information. However, current approaches face notable challenges, including the difficulty in obtaining large-scale and unbiased medical datasets, significant privacy concerns, and inefficiencies due to manual dataset annotation. To address these issues, This study introduce a novel methodology leveraging publicly accessible online health forums to systematically build an unbiased, privacy-conscious QA dataset, and it employs Topic-guided Semantic Modeling (TGSM) for automated topic identification, enabling efficient and targeted annotation of relevant patient-generated content. Subsequently, this study propose a two-stage QA pipeline based on a Retriever-Reader architecture, which is further enhanced through fine-tuning state-of-the-art transformer-based models on the constructed domain-specific QA dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our fine-tuned BioBERT significantly outperforms existing benchmarks, offering accurate patient-derived insights and providing a replicable framework for building efficient medical QA systems.
item.dc:creator: Zhipeng Yin, Zichong Wang, Min Chen, Ian Stockwell, Xin Ning, Jun Liu, Wenbin Zhang

item.title: Self-Evolving Dual-Role Deliberation for Medication Recommendation from Clinical Records
item.description: Recommending medications from electronic health records (EHRs) is a safety-critical task that demands therapeutic coverage, explicit safety constraints, traceable justification, and continual adaptivity. Supervised neural models freeze at deployment and cannot reason about new phenotypes, while existing LLM pipelines are single-pass and lack a cross-case improvement loop. We propose SEMPA, a training-free agentic framework that couples a Proposer with a Critic in multi-round adversarial deliberation, grounds candidates with molecular-aware retrieval, contrastively evolves both agents' natural-language policies under a semantic-anchor constraint, and enforces rule-based DDI and contraindication checks. On 100 MIMIC-IV encounters, SEMPA reaches 0.3116 Jaccard, 0.7295 F1, and a 0.0172 DDI rate, improving F1 by 57.7% and cutting DDI by 77.5% over the strongest supervised baseline. Two LLM judges rank SEMPA highest, and six-backbone studies confirm that gains derive from the framework rather than a specific model.
item.dc:creator: Jiyue Jiang, Yu Lei, Yitao Xu, Zikang Wang, Zhenyu Wang, Licheng Zong, Han Huang, Ziyi Li, Zhiyu Huo, Yuhan Chen, Jiayang Chen, Xiaodan Fan, Yu Li

item.title: Automating literature screening and knowledge synthesis with large language models
item.description: Scientific literature is expanding rapidly, yet much of its knowledge remains difficult to organize and reuse due to the substantial workload needed to navigate large, heterogeneous literature corpora. Here, we develop a generalizable large language model (LLM)-powered framework that automates literature screening, structured information extraction, and knowledge synthesis within a unified workflow. We benchmarked 11 state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight LLMs across three materials science screening tasks differing in scope, corpus size, and class imbalance. Seven LLMs achieved balanced accuracies above 0.90 across all tasks, with the best-performing LLM reaching 0.96--0.98, demonstrating the potential of LLMs to accurately screen large, highly imbalanced scientific corpora. The framework also substantially reduces manual effort, screening 10,000 records within four minutes compared with approximately 83 person-hours for manual screening. Beyond literature screening, the framework extracts structured information from full-text articles, enabling content-level quantification of research landscapes that extends traditional bibliometric analysis based on publication metadata. This capability reveals methodological trends and underexplored directions, as shown for machine learning in concrete materials science. We further demonstrate its utility for information and data discovery by identifying publications containing silicate glass density data that are difficult to retrieve using conventional search strategies, which can support downstream hypothesis development, research design, and data-driven scientific discovery. Overall, these results demonstrate the broad applicability of LLM-powered literature analysis across scientific domains and its potential to transform large, unstructured literature corpora into structured, analyzable knowledge at scale.
item.dc:creator: Zhanzhao Li, Qiyao He, Weiqiang Chen, Kengran Yang, Kai Gong

item.title: Human vs Machine Translation Detection: A Cross-Model, Cross-Domain, and Low-Resource Analysis
item.description: The growing reliance on web-crawled corpora for training large language models introduces a critical challenge: machine-translated (MT) content is often treated as human translation (HT), potentially degrading data quality and propagating synthetic artifacts, especially in low-resource settings. In this work, we study MT-HT detectability across high-resource (English, Spanish) and low-resource (Swahili, Afrikaans) languages using both decoder-only LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot settings, and fine-tuned multilingual encoders trained at the sentence level and on token-chunked inputs. We find that decoder-only models provide limited discrimination overall and exhibit a consistent class-asymmetric failure mode: they recognize human-written text reliably (high HT recall) but rarely flag fluent machine output (low MT recall). Encoder-based classifiers achieve high accuracy when evaluated on data generated by the same MT systems and translators used during training in a legislative domain, but their MT recall drops sharply on unseen translators and on unseen domains such as low-resource conversational text and medical content. To address this limitation, we evaluate models on longer inputs by chunking text into segments of up to 300 tokens, which substantially improves generalization, suggesting that sentence-level signals are insufficient for robust detection. Finally, we analyze the relationship between translation quality and detectability using COMET and BLEURT, showing that lower-quality MT is more easily identified, while high-quality MT remains difficult to distinguish from HT. Our results highlight the importance of input granularity, translator generalization, and translation quality in building robust MT detection systems across domains and languages.
item.dc:creator: Yabsera Yemanberhan, Prasenjit Mitra, Roald Eiselen

item.title: TRIAGE-CPG: A Cross-Model Study of Budgeted Static Malware Triage with Large Language Models
item.description: When triaging unknown binaries, security analysts must decide which samples to clear as benign, flag as malicious, or escalate for deeper analysis. Large Language Models (LLMs) could support these decisions by interpreting decompiled code, but a binary can contain hundreds or thousands of functions, making exhaustive LLM analysis impractical. We study how current LLMs behave when static triage is formulated as budgeted evidence acquisition: which functions they inspect and how they trade off benign clearance, malware detection, and escalation. To enable a controlled comparison, we implement TRIAGE-CPG, a fixed pipeline over a code property graph (CPG) of a decompiled binary. An LLM-free heuristic selects seed functions, an agent expands the resulting evidence dossier under a fixed budget, and a reporting stage produces a benign, suspicious, or malicious verdict together with a behavioral report. We evaluate eight closed-source and open-weight models on 1,000 Windows PE binaries, using a 600-sample test split and the same zero-shot protocol for every model. We assess the ternary verdicts under both a strict binary reading and triage balanced accuracy (tBA), which credits malware that is flagged or escalated and benign samples only when cleared. After analyzing about 40 of a mean 1,000 functions per binary, the highest-scoring model reaches a strict balanced accuracy of 0.805 and a tBA of 0.855, flagging 65% of malware, escalating another 12%, and clearing 94% of benign samples. The models implement different triage policies: high-specificity models produce small, malware-rich escalation queues, whereas recall-oriented models escalate or flag much more broadly. Both closed-source and open-weight models appear across this spectrum. Our results identify no universal deployment configuration: model choice itself determines the clear/flag/escalate trade-off under limited static evidence.

item.title: Agent-Native by Design: A Programming Language for Agentic Applications
item.description: Building agentic applications requires combining large language model (LLM) operations, workflow structure and application state, and model-guided routing. With SDKs and agent frameworks, developers connect these components through supporting code that prepares model inputs, propagates state, and dispatches model-selected steps. Workflow changes can require coordinated updates to this code, increasing development and testing effort. Splitting execution logic between application code and framework internals also limits compiler visibility into control flow and state dependencies, hindering automatic optimization. We introduce Agent-Native Programming, which unifies these three components with shared execution semantics. We realize this approach in Jac, a Python-superset language, through "by llm()" for typed model operations and tool use, Object-Spatial Programming for workflow structure and state, and "visit ... by llm()" for model-guided routing. The routing construct derives the model's choices from executable workflow steps and schedules the selected steps. This explicit connection between model decisions and program execution gives the compiler and runtime a common basis for dependency analysis and automatic optimization. Across five benchmarks and five baselines, Jac achieves a 1.8-8.7x reduction in AI-integration code relative to the OpenAI SDK, with competitive observed task quality and lower coding-agent development effort. Two case studies demonstrate speculative execution and service partitioning through configuration alone, using program analysis and runtime checks to preserve workflow behavior under stated conditions.

item.title: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces
item.description: Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence

item.title: What Makes a Good Move? Learning to Act from Experience in Visual Worlds
item.description: Learning visual policies requires turning interaction experience into guidance for individual decisions. Trajectory outcomes obscure action quality, while unguided exploration can revisit familiar situations. We present \textsc{LightAct}, an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. Interaction segments are summarized into experience entries and consolidated into a game-specific skill that guides root collection toward broader state coverage. At each root, candidate actions are compared through short rollouts under a shared frozen policy. Environment-reported score gains are averaged across continuations and normalized into relative action rewards, producing reusable supervision for reinforcement learning. Policy training uses a compact dataset of just 1,024 decision roots collected in a single source game and paired with their action rewards. Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, \textsc{LightAct} improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales, respectively, with our strongest model competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Ablations show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance and consistent gains across three policy optimizers. Case studies show how rollouts distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

item.title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
item.description: Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.
item.dc:creator: Zhen Xu, Hang Yin, Zitao Zhang, Kevin Zhao, Xuefeng Liu

item.title: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering
item.description: As large language models (LLMs) evolve from conversational assistants into autonomous agents embedded in software development workflows, estimating their environmental footprint requires moving beyond conventional token-based accounting. Existing energy estimators focus on isolated request-response interactions, overlooking the repeated processing of accumulated context, cache reuse, and work delegated to subagents. We analyze nearly one billion tokens collected across 42 sessions and 752 task episodes over ten weeks of real-world AI-assisted software development. Cached-context reads make up 94.8% of all API-reported tokens, while uncached input accounts for only 0.017%; for every generated token, approximately 260 cached tokens are read. Context grows 5.3-fold over a session compared with 1.4-fold within individual tasks. To quantify the energy implications, we extend an existing analytical inference-energy model to account for cached-context processing, yielding a cache-aware hybrid estimator. It estimates approximately 250 kWh for the workload, compared with approximately 10 kWh from the output-based estimator EcoLogits, a 25-fold difference largely driven by cached-context reads. Neither estimator has been validated on long cached contexts, but no modeling assumption we varied closes the gap. Starting each task from a fresh context would lower our estimate by about 60%. We also find that parent-session logs report only a subagent's final internal call, undercounting delegated tokens by a factor of ten; for this workload the correction changes the energy estimate by about 5%, but token-volume studies are fully exposed to it. Our findings expose a substantial gap between how current energy estimators and agentic workloads treat context, highlighting the need for workflow-level energy accounting that captures context accumulation, cache reuse, and delegated execution.

item.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
item.description: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

item.title: Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache
item.description: Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.
item.dc:creator: Saksham Gupta, Michael Li

item.title: One-Shot Calibration via Model Editing
item.description: Model editing aims to correct errors in large, pretrained models by replacing model generations with user-provided responses. Existing editors assume a single target answer for each edit. However, many real tasks inherently entail uncertainty, resulting in multiple plausible answers with varying likelihoods in user feedback. Such feedback forms a target distribution to not only correct but also calibrate model generations. We therefore propose SoftEdit, the first model editor to leverage uncertainty in user responses and perform one-shot calibration during editing. To generalize calibration to unseen samples, SoftEdit uses co-plausibility relationships between answers while preserving real distributional shifts, balancing the new distributional generality-locality tradeoff. Across three language models, three vision-language models, and two large datasets, SoftEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, ultimately showing that uncertainty in user responses enables generalizable calibration of pretrained models beyond single-answer corrections.

item.title: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
item.description: A Koopman controller can stabilize its learned latent-space linear model yet fail to stabilize the nonlinear plant. The learned model propagates predictions in latent space, while the deployed controller repeatedly re-encodes the measured physical state. We show that nominal closed-loop stability transfers to the nonlinear plant when the learned and true closed-loop dynamics agree to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We derive a robustness margin for approximate matching and show that a stable open-loop latent model cannot exactly match an unstable equilibrium. We introduce Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and enforces first-order matching to this estimate. TIK recovers the fitted LQR gain at the target, while a bilinear predictor captures state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. Across four simulated unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers have stable latent closed loops, but their deployed nonlinear systems are locally unstable. In contrast, all 40 TIK controllers locally stabilize their respective nonlinear plants. An offline stability test using empirical curvature estimates identifies stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems, but is inconclusive under high noise. Under explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction after entry under local feedback. TIK achieves 88\% constrained cart-pole swing-up success with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1-5 ms per step.
